body_text: View All News Dexcom Reports First Quarter 2026 Financial Results April 30, 2026 SAN DIEGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- DexCom, Inc. (Nasdaq: DXCM) today reported its financial results as of and for the quarter ended March 31, 2026. First Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights: Revenue grew 15% year-over-year to $1.192 billion on a reported basis and 12% year-over-year on an organic 1 basis. U.S. revenue grew 11% and international revenue grew 26% on a reported basis and 17% on an organic 1 basis, all on a year-over-year basis. GAAP operating income of $255.3 million or 21.4% of revenue, an increase of 850 basis points compared to the first quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP operating income* of $264.4 million or 22.2% of reported revenue, an increase of 840 basis points compared to the first quarter of 2025. First Quarter 2026 Strategic Highlights: Expanded the launch of Dexcom G7 15 Day CGM across all channels in the United States. Introduced enhanced Smart Meal Logging features to the Stelo platform. Showcased extensive clinical evidence at ATTD 2026, including one-year registry data demonstrating that Dexcom G7 delivered significant improvement in A1C for people with type 2 diabetes who are not on insulin therapy. “Dexcom delivered strong revenue growth and margin performance to start the year, reflecting healthy demand for Dexcom CGM and continued operational improvement,” said Jake Leach, Dexcom’s president and CEO. “We will work to build on this momentum throughout 2026 and look forward to highlighting Dexcom’s long-term growth opportunity at our Investor Day in the coming weeks.” 2026 Annual Guidance Dexcom is raising fiscal year 2026 guidance for Non-GAAP Operating Margin and Adjusted EBITDA Margin, and reiterating guidance for Revenue and Non-GAAP Gross Profit Margin at the following levels: Revenue of $5.16 - $5.25 billion (approximately 11-13% growth) Non-GAAP Gross Profit Margin of approximately 63-64% Non-GAAP Operating Margin of approximately 23-23.5% Adjusted EBITDA Margin of approximately 31-31.5% ____________________ 1 First quarter 2026 organic revenue was $1.165 billion and excludes $26.6 million of foreign exchange impact. First Quarter 2026 Financial Results Revenue: In the first quarter of 2026, worldwide revenue grew 15% to $1.192 billion on a reported basis, up from $1.036 billion in the first quarter of 2025. Gross Profit: GAAP gross profit totaled $750.3 million or 62.9% of revenue for the first quarter of 2026, compared to $589.0 million or 56.9% of revenue in the first quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP gross profit* totaled $757.4 million or 63.5% of reported revenue for the first quarter of 2026, compared to $596.2 million or 57.5% of reported revenue in the first quarter of 2025. Operating Income: GAAP operating income for the first quarter of 2026 was $255.3 million or 21.4% of revenue, compared to GAAP operating income of $133.7 million or 12.9% of revenue for the first quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP operating income* for the first quarter of 2026 was $264.4 million or 22.2% of reported revenue, compared to non-GAAP operating income of $143.1 million or 13.8% of reported revenue for the first quarter of 2025. Net Income and Diluted Net Income Per Share: GAAP net income was $199.5 million, or $0.51 per diluted share, for the first quarter of 2026, compared to GAAP net income of $105.4 million, or $0.27 per diluted share, for the first quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP net income* was $216.3 million, or $0.56 per diluted share, for the first quarter of 2026, compared to non-GAAP net income of $127.7 million, or $0.32 per diluted share, for the first quarter of 2025. The first quarter 2026 non-GAAP net income excludes $8.0 million of amortization of intangible assets, $1.1 million of business transition and other significant items, and $7.7 million of tax adjustments. Cash and Liquidity: As of March 31, 2026, Dexcom held $2.42 billion in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities and our revolving credit facility remains undrawn. The cash balance represents significant financial and strategic flexibility as Dexcom continues to expand production capacity and explore new market opportunities. * See Table D below for a reconciliation of these GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures. The link to the webcast will be available on the Dexcom Investor Relations website at investors.dexcom.com by navigating to “Events and Presentations,” and will be archived for future reference. To listen to the conference call, please dial (888) 414-4585 (U.S./Canada) or (646) 960-0331 (International) and use the confirmation ID “9430114” approximately five minutes prior to the start time. title: Composable Schemas is GA
summary: Composable schemas are now generally available in SpiceDB 1.51.1. Split monolithic schemas into well-defined, reusable components so teams can move faster, make changes, and scale without everything becoming entangled.
body_text: In a blog post from December 2024 we announced that we had developed the initial foundations for composable schemas. Today, I'm excited to share that composable schemas are now generally available in SpiceDB 1.51.1. What are Composable Schemas? Composable schemas allow you to better manage and modularize your large schemas, which helps organizations scale. It also enables the open source community to design reusable data models for common problems and schema structures. In practice, large schemas tend to become monolithic. Composable schemas solve this by enabling you to split your schema into well-defined, reusable components, so teams can move faster, make changes, and scale without everything becoming entangled. Just as importantly, this modular approach unlocks new possibilities for the open source community, making it easier to share, reuse, and build on common authorization patterns rather than reinventing them from scratch. "AuthZed's composable schemas have been a blessing and have helped us better manage authorization at scale. Instead of wrestling with one massive monolithic schema, we're now breaking things into clean, reusable pieces that are actually readable and reflect how our systems and core components are built. It's made the development workflow faster, safer, and much easier to work with." — Simon Bruno, Senior Security Engineer at Forter How To Use Composable Schemas The composable schemas feature required significant changes in our schema compiler around making it filesystem-aware so that, if an error occurs, we can tell you exactly which file contains the error. For similar reasons, we also updated our Language Server Protocol, which is used by the VS Code extension, to be filesystem-aware. There are two breaking changes compared to the Preview to be aware of: use import is now required if you want to use import "foo.zed" syntax. use partial is now required if you want to declare or reference partials. In order to enhance the developer experience, we have made a number of changes to our tooling, namely: We released the Zed CLI to v1. The various zed commands now support composable schemas. For example: zed validate <root.zed> is what you can call to validate across multiple files. It will resolve your imports and validate those files as well. zed schema compile <root.zed> is what will combine the multiple files back into one schema that you can then write in SpiceDB. We released VS Code extension 1.1.1 to work with composable schemas. For example, when you are hovering over a definition (or a caveat, or a partial) that is declared in another file, you will get the right tooltip; or if you press F12 to navigate to a definition, it will navigate to the file that declared it. Note that our playground does not support import syntax as the Playground uses a singular editor (and doesn't support the notion of files). But let us know if this is something that you would like us to support! Thank You, SpiceDB Community We would like to thank the community for your patience in releasing this, and for your bug reports that allowed us to make a better experience for everyone. If you run into issues or would like to request a feature, open an issue or hit us up in our Discord server . Happy modeling! On this page What are Composable Schemas? title: Actinium Pharmaceuticals Announces New Pan-Tumor Preclinical Data for ATNM-400 in Solid Tumors and Differentiated Mechanism for Actimab-A in AML to be Presented at 2026 AACR Annual Meeting

summary: Becoming a volunteer for UPchieve is truly one of the most rewarding things I have done. body_text: Written by Nai, a high school senior and UPchieve volunteer tutor. We love sharing student voices to highlight the impact and perspective of young people giving back. How It All Began Becoming a volunteer for UPchieve is truly one of the most rewarding things I have done. When I first started volunteering, I wasn’t sure what to expect, as I had never tutored outside of my close friends at school. I did, however, know I wanted to give back to my community and use the skills I've learned in school to help others, which is why joining UPchieve was the perfect decision for me. What is UPchieve? UPchieve is an online platform where volunteers get connected with students who need free academic support. It’s simple to get started as a tutor; you can easily make an account, go through quick training, complete certification quizzes in the areas you would like to tutor, and start tutoring. Once you get started, though, there is a lot more to learn besides the content you’re teaching. Each student who logs on to request support is different. The way they learn, their personalities, and how they are feeling about the content. Some students log on super overwhelmed by an exam, an assignment, or even just a concept they don’t understand. Others just need reassurance that they understand the material and maybe need some one-on-one practice to feel better. Regardless, it’s important to know how to handle other people's emotions and be able to guide them through what they’re feeling so that they can feel comfortable learning. My Experience with UPchieve In my experience as a volunteer tutor with UPchieve, I learned that each student is different and has unique characteristics as well as diverse ways of learning. One session that sticks with me was with a student who needed help in Algebra 2. At first, they were really unsure about where to start and how to approach the questions. When I asked them how they came to the answer they wrote down, their answers were short and unclear. At first, I didn’t know how to handle their reactions, but then I thought back to when I was in their position, learning this subject for the first time and feeling confused and stressed as well. I remembered how it feels to not understand things sometimes and how much confidence one can gain by having the tutor’s patience and understanding. From then on, I took a moment to slow things down rather than rushing through my methods. Instead of looking into their homework questions right away, we started by going over the concepts and formulas together. We even created fun ways to remember things and drew pictures when needed. After doing this, the student went from short answers to engaging in the conversation and actively asking questions. After we had gotten through reviewing the basic concepts, they were already doing the homework problems on their own based on what they had just learned. And by the end of the session, their homework was completed, and they had a much better understanding of the concepts. Seeing the students' attitude change from the start to the end of the session was when I realized that tutoring is so much more than just teaching. It’s about giving the student confidence and understanding to be able to learn and complete things on their own. What I’ve learned Tutoring on UPchieve has been so much more to me than just helping others. It has helped me grow as a person as well. I’ve learned how to change my communication style based on each student, how to ask the right questions to figure out how a student is feeling or thinking, and how to be a little more patient even when things are moving slower than I thought. This experience has taught me more about empathy and patience, which motivated me to pick up more tutoring requests and work with new students on UPcheive. Looking back, I'm beyond grateful that I chose to join UPchieve, and each session is a reminder that the smallest acts of giving back can change someone's academic journey. I’ve definitely seen firsthand that having access to a free and caring tutor is life-changing for these students and that, at the end of the day, is the most important and rewarding thing. Tips for Future Volunteers Starting out may feel intimidating, but it’s less scary than it seems. Here are a few things I’ve learned: Any knowledge helps. You don’t need all the answers, guiding and encouraging students is often enough. Be patient and kind. Breaking concepts down, organizing tasks, or just offering reassurance can make a huge difference. Don’t overthink it. Go in with an open mind, listen carefully, and focus on helping the student move forward. Want to Volunteer? Are you interested in volunteering to help students as well? Check out UPchieve’s volunteering steps page to learn more and get started to make an impact today. About the Author Nai, Class of 2026, has been teaching multiple subjects on UPchieve since her junior year. When tutoring, she enjoys helping students build confidence in their learning.

title: Does a Pool Help or Hurt Your Home Value?
summary: Thinking about building a pool? Discover whether swimming pools increase home value, what buyers look for, and when a pool can boost resale value.
body_text: If you’re dreaming of morning laps and poolside cocktails — but are worried that installing a pool could hurt your home’s resale value — you’ll need to consider factors like your area’s climate, potential buyer profiles, the norms of other homes in your neighborhood, and more. In this guide, we’ll walk you through the most important considerations for how a pool affects home value, the pool features that can add the most value to your home, and when a pool might not be the right investment. Athens 13.37 Fiberglass Pool How Much Value Can a Swimming Pool Add to Your Home? The exact amount of resale value a pool can add to your home will fluctuate depending on the size, shape, design, and condition of your pool, as well as the demand in your local market. However, based on 2025 statistics noted by real estate platform Redfin, most homeowners can expect to see approximately a 7% increase in their home’s value after installing a pool. For example, if your property is worth $500,000, you can expect a roughly $35,000 bump in your value after installing a pool. However, while your property value has gone up, it’s important to distinguish this number from the financial return on investment (ROI) when it comes to recouping the installation cost. Your installation price will vary depending on the design of your pool and the contractor you choose for the work. If your pool is designed well, has premium features that are attractive to buyers, and is well-maintained, your pool could add even more value than expected. This can offset more of the up-front costs and give you a better ROI. Conversely, if your pool is poorly designed for the space or needs repairs at the time of sale, you’ll likely see a lower ROI. 4 Situations Where a Pool Consistently Boosts Home Value So, when does a pool increase home value? Let’s look at some examples of factors that will weigh heavily on resale value and what it could mean for your backyard: Climate and Geography: The Most Important Factor While fiberglass pools can absolutely be a solid investment for summer enjoyment in cold climate areas, it’s undeniable that warm and humid climates turn pools from a luxury into an in-demand feature. Areas like the Southeastern and Southwestern U.S. can have warm temperatures year-round, making pools an attractive prospect for beating the brutal heat that can come in summer and early fall. For instance, Phoenix, Arizona is largely considered the hottest city in the United States with an average summer temperature of 93.7℉ and an annual average temperature of 75.4℉. In 2024, Phoenix experienced an unprecedented 113 consecutive days with temperatures of at least 100 degrees — and it’s only getting warmer. However, this means that pools are extremely alluring to home buyers. In fact, as many as 32.7% of all homes in Phoenix, AZ have a pool in the backyard, proving that the climate can be a significant factor in how a pool affects home value. Neighborhood Norms: Is a Pool Expected? Think about what the norms are when it comes to pools in your neighborhood, aligning your vision for your backyard with future buyer expectations. For example, if you live in a high-end neighborhood where pools are seen as an expected luxury feature, not having one can be a disadvantage because it doesn’t match what the market typically expects. However, this doesn’t mean that pools are only valuable in high-end neighborhoods where most houses have pools installed. In neighborhoods where pools are less common, having one can be a differentiator between your home and competitors in the area. Home Buyer Profiles A pool’s value will be weighted heavily on the target buyer demographic in your market. Different buyer profiles will see the same features differently. One set of buyers could see a pool as the perfect place to relax after a hard day, envisioning laps in the pool in lieu of the gym and throwing parties to meet their new neighbors. However, another set of buyers could see the same pool as another chore to take care of, weighing the costs and time commitment of maintaining it more heavily than the benefits. Your home’s value with a pool will be different to both potential groups, so it’s important that you partner with a real estate agent who knows how to market your pool to the right buyer profile. High Demand in the Local Market Much of your home’s overall resale value is dictated by the local market, and buyer demand will change how features like pools are viewed. In a seller’s market, pools can often be seen as a desirable feature that brings a feeling of luxury to a home, especially in areas where buyers have fewer available choices. In a buyer’s market, where there is more choice for properties and neighborhoods, sellers will often need to strategically position their homes for buyers by looking at the lifestyle expectations that come with owning a pool. Fiji Fiberglass | Ocean Blue Crystite Crystal Pool Features That Help Maximize Resale Value While the influences above play a factor in how a swimming pool impacts home resale value, there are other elements to consider that can help maximize your return. A well-maintained pool with careful design considerations will be seen as significantly different from one that was incorrectly installed or experienced a lapse in care. Here are some of the pool features that can add the most value to your home: Inground vs. Above-Ground Pools Inground and semi-inground pools are the only pool types that add significant value to a home, and are typically the only pools included in appraisals. This is because above-ground pools are generally considered temporary structures, and many buyers even expect them to be removed before closing. Fiberglass and vinyl liner pools are often more attractive to buyers than those made from concrete because of their lower maintenance commitments, which can significantly lower their long-term costs. Unlike concrete , fiberglass and vinyl liner pools don’t need expensive resurfacing, and their flexible materials and non-porous surfaces make them more resistant to algae growth and groundwater retention that can lead to costly repair work. Condition and Maintenance are Critical The condition of your pool and its surrounding area is critical for your home’s resale value. Having a well-maintained pool with clear, sparkling water and beautiful landscaping can create a valuable first impression on buyers and make it easy for them to envision themselves enjoying your backyard as their own. However, a neglected pool can be seen as a liability instead of an investment. Buyers can be more likely to imagine repair costs and hours spent on maintenance instead of relaxing poolside. It can’t be overstated how critical a clean and well-maintained pool is for resale value. You could install a beautifully designed pool with the most sought-after features, and it could actually lower your home’s value if the water is full of debris or green with algae. Aesthetic Appeal and Backyard Balance A pool is just one part of your backyard. Having an overall space that is aesthetically pleasing and proportional will increase your property value more than simply having a pool. A pool that is integrated seamlessly with the rest of the backyard will create a space where buyers can imagine options for themselves. For instance, a buyer might see a pool with an attached kitchen and think about how they could host guests without running back and forth from the rest of the house. Or, they could notice a well-proportioned backyard and get excited at the possibility of having enough room for cocktails by the pool while children play on the rest of the lawn. When a Pool Can Hurt Your Home’s Value Although there are many pros to owning a pool, there are some instances where it can hurt your property value. Let’s go over some of the reasons why a buyer could see a pool as a burden, not a benefit: The Liability and Expense Deterrent Potential buyers can come to a showing pre-disposed to high-cost concerns when it comes to pools. Although fiberglass and vinyl liner pools require significantly less maintenance than concrete, they still require regular maintenance to look and perform their best. This can be a cost that some buyers simply don’t want to take on, despite the exercise and lifestyle benefits a pool can offer. Pools also often cause higher homeowner insurance premiums due to the potential liability concerns. Pools are considered an “ attractive nuisance ” by the insurance industry, which is anything that might attract a child and pose a danger to an unsupervised child, such as trampolines, treehouses, and power tools. Market and Buyer Resistance Certain buyers and markets have more resistance to pools than others. This often includes young families with small children who might try to avoid pools due to safety concerns. There will also likely be fewer buyers in northern areas and cold climates where pools are closed for longer periods during the year. Radiant Freeform Semi-inground Pool Preparing Your Pool Home for Resale If you’re getting ready to put your home on the market, you’ll want to make sure your pool area is clean and presentable to be attractive to potential buyers. Here are some steps you can take to prepare your backyard for when you’re ready to sell your home: Clean Your Pool Area Thoroughly: Remove any debris from the water, scrub the pool walls, and treat your water so it’s clear and sparkling when buyers come to tour the space. You should also clean all equipment and the surrounding areas, like the deck and patio. Be Proactive With Safety Measures: Some buyers’ skepticism of pools is rooted in safety concerns, especially among young families with children. You can proactively head off those worries by updating your pool with fencing, self-latching gates, safety barriers, and alarms that serve as layers of protection for the pool area and maintain compliance with state and local pool laws. Update Landscaping: Trim hedges and tree limbs, replace struggling or dead potted plants, and be sure all lawn equipment is properly stored to keep the space looking organized. Think about adding colorful tropical plants that create a vacation vibe, such as potted palms, banana trees, and birds of paradise. Stage Your “Backyard Paradise”: You want to make the surrounding area look as inviting as possible so potential buyers see themselves enjoying the space as their own. Stage the pool area with loungers, chaises, and comfortable patio furniture that lends itself to entertaining and relaxation. Hire the Right Realtor: Your realtor is your home’s spokesperson and biggest cheerleader. Look for someone with experience marketing homes with pools who knows how to sell their benefits. The Final Verdict on Pool Resale Value The total impact of a swimming pool on home resale value often comes with a complex answer. A pool is largely a lifestyle investment, not a guaranteed financial one. Much of a pool’s contribution to your home’s value is determined by factors that are largely outside of your control, such as the local market and individual buyer opinions and preconceptions about pool ownership. Instead of focusing primarily on what your pool will eventually bring to someone else who buys your home in the future, think about what makes you excited about enjoying a pool today . While it’s responsible to keep your property value in mind, it’s equally important that you enjoy your backyard to the fullest, whether it’s a space for you to unwind and meditate, or one where you plan to spend time with the people you love most. It depends! Homes with pools in areas with warm climates are often in demand year-round because they provide comfort, fun, and a reprieve from hot and humid weather. However, many factors come into play that can affect the sale of a house, including local market changes, buyer preferences, and neighborhood norms. However, they can add a lifestyle ROI that can’t be beaten, especially for families with children who want to make core memories and those who value impressive, design-forward additions to their homes. Does removing an old, broken pool decrease property value? Removing an old, broken pool can actually increase your property value, especially if removal is completed by a reputable professional and you take care to update your yard with landscaping after. title: Cómo elegir la mejor cotización de un seguro de carga
summary: Aprende a elegir la mejor cotización de un seguro de carga para proteger tus mercancías frente a robos, daños o pérdidas. Descubre los factores clave, tipos de pólizas y cómo evaluar proveedores para garantizar la estabilidad financiera y continuidad de tu operación logística.
body_text: El transporte de mercancías, tanto a nivel nacional como internacional, está lleno de riesgos inherentes que pueden comprometer la seguridad y entrega de los productos. Estos riesgos incluyen desde pérdidas parciales o totales, daños durante el trayecto, robo de mercancía o retrasos que pueden impactar negativamente en la cadena de suministro y en la relación con los clientes. Las empresas, especialmente aquellas que manejan grandes volúmenes de bienes o productos de alto valor, deben contar con una estrategia de mitigación de estos riesgos, siendo el seguro de carga una de las herramientas más esenciales en la protección logística. Contar con un seguro de carga no solo protege el valor de los bienes transportados, sino que también asegura la estabilidad financiera de la empresa en caso de eventos adversos. Sin embargo, seleccionar la mejor cotización para un seguro de carga puede ser un proceso complejo. Existen múltiples variables que deben evaluarse para garantizar que se obtiene la protección adecuada sin incurrir en costos excesivos. Entre estos factores se incluyen las coberturas específicas que ofrece cada póliza (daños físicos, pérdida total, robo, etc.), las exclusiones que podrían dejar ciertos riesgos sin protección, los costos asociados a las primas y el deducible, así como servicios adicionales que puedan agregar valor, como la gestión eficiente de reclamaciones o el acceso a asesoramiento personalizado. En este artículo, no solo te guiaremos paso a paso en la elección de la cotización más adecuada para tu seguro de carga, sino que también exploraremos estrategias para optimizar los costos y asegurar que las necesidades específicas de tu operación logística estén completamente cubiertas. Así, podrás tomar decisiones más informadas, logrando un equilibrio entre costo y cobertura, y garantizando la seguridad y continuidad de tus operaciones frente a cualquier eventualidad. ¿Qué es un seguro de carga? Un seguro de carga es una herramienta fundamental en el mundo del transporte de mercancías, ya que ofrece una cobertura integral frente a los diversos riesgos que pueden surgir durante el traslado de productos. Este tipo de seguro está diseñado para proteger las mercancías frente a daños, pérdidas o incluso robos que pueden ocurrir durante su transporte, ya sea terrestre, marítimo o aéreo. La importancia de este seguro radica en que no solo resguarda los bienes en tránsito, sino que también garantiza la estabilidad financiera de las empresas, especialmente aquellas que operan en el comercio internacional, donde los riesgos son mayores y las operaciones más complejas. Las empresas que participan en la cadena de suministro global, así como aquellas que realizan envíos a nivel nacional, dependen de un seguro de carga para mitigar posibles pérdidas económicas. Sin esta cobertura, las empresas corren el riesgo de enfrentarse a grandes gastos imprevistos que pueden afectar gravemente su operación. Un ejemplo claro es el daño a mercancías perecederas, que deben llegar en condiciones óptimas a su destino. Sin un seguro adecuado, el costo de estos productos dañados recaería completamente en la empresa transportadora o en el propietario de la mercancía. Existen diferentes tipos de seguros de carga, cuya cobertura varía en función del medio de transporte y del tipo de mercancía transportada. Estos son algunos de los más comunes: Seguro de transporte marítimo: este tipo de seguro cubre los daños o pérdidas que puedan sufrir las mercancías durante su transporte por vía marítima. Es común en operaciones internacionales, dado que el transporte marítimo es uno de los medios más utilizados para el comercio global. Este seguro puede cubrir desde daños por tormentas y condiciones climáticas adversas, hasta hundimientos, incendios o pérdidas totales de la mercancía. Seguro de transporte terrestre: diseñado para proteger las mercancías que son transportadas por carretera o ferrocarril. Este seguro es crucial para operaciones a nivel nacional y transfronterizo, especialmente en regiones donde las carreteras pueden ser inseguras o donde existe una alta incidencia de robos. Además, cubre daños por accidentes de tráfico, incendios, robos o eventos climáticos extremos que afecten el traslado de la mercancía. Seguro de transporte aéreo: este seguro protege contra los riesgos asociados con el transporte de mercancías por vía aérea. Debido a la rapidez del transporte aéreo, este seguro es especialmente útil para productos de alto valor o de naturaleza perecedera, que deben llegar rápidamente a su destino. Entre los riesgos cubiertos por este tipo de seguro se incluyen accidentes aéreos, pérdida de equipaje o daños causados durante el manejo de la mercancía en aeropuertos. Además de estos tipos de seguro, las pólizas pueden adaptarse a las necesidades específicas de cada empresa, dependiendo de los productos que manejen y de las rutas que utilicen. Las empresas pueden optar por pólizas que cubran envíos únicos o pólizas anuales que cubren múltiples operaciones durante todo el año, lo que permite una mayor flexibilidad en su gestión de riesgos. En cualquier caso, contar con un seguro de carga adecuado es una decisión clave para proteger la inversión, mantener la competitividad y asegurar el éxito a largo plazo de cualquier empresa involucrada en el transporte de mercancías. Factores clave a considerar al cotizar un seguro de carga Al solicitar cotizaciones para un seguro de carga, es importante tener en cuenta varios factores para garantizar que la póliza cubra todos los aspectos necesarios de tu operación logística. Aquí te detallamos los más relevantes: 1. Tipo de mercancía El tipo de mercancía que se transporta es uno de los principales factores que influirán en la cotización del seguro. Las compañías aseguradoras evalúan el riesgo de acuerdo con la naturaleza de los productos. Por ejemplo, productos perecederos, electrónicos o mercancías de alto valor, como joyería, suelen tener primas más altas debido a su vulnerabilidad a daños o robos. 2. Modo de transporte El modo de transporte (terrestre, aéreo o marítimo) también afecta el costo del seguro. Generalmente, el transporte marítimo y aéreo tiene primas más altas que el transporte terrestre, ya que los riesgos asociados, como tormentas o accidentes aéreos, son mayores. Además, ciertos modos de transporte requieren coberturas especiales, como el seguro de contenedores para el transporte marítimo. 3. Coberturas y exclusiones No todas las pólizas ofrecen las mismas coberturas. Es esencial analizar qué eventos específicos cubre el seguro de carga. Las coberturas comunes incluyen: Daños físicos a la mercancía. Robo o hurto durante el transporte. Pérdida de mercancía. Por otro lado, también es vital revisar las exclusiones de la póliza. Algunas pólizas no cubren daños por empaques inadecuados, errores de documentación o retrasos en la entrega. Asegúrate de entender claramente qué no cubre el seguro para evitar sorpresas desagradables en caso de un siniestro. 4. Valor asegurado El valor asegurado es el monto máximo que la aseguradora pagará en caso de pérdida o daño de la mercancía. Es importante calcular el valor asegurado en función del valor real de los bienes transportados, teniendo en cuenta no solo el costo de los productos, sino también los costos asociados al transporte, como los impuestos y los aranceles. 5. Deductibles Los seguros de carga suelen incluir un deducible, que es el monto que la empresa asegurada debe pagar antes de que la aseguradora cubra el resto del siniestro. A mayor deducible, generalmente, menor será la prima del seguro. Sin embargo, debes asegurarte de que el deducible sea asequible para tu empresa en caso de un incidente. Evaluación de proveedores de seguros de carga Elegir el proveedor adecuado para el seguro de carga no es una decisión que deba tomarse a la ligera, ya que la protección de tus mercancías y la estabilidad financiera de tu empresa pueden depender de esta elección. Los proveedores de seguros de carga varían en términos de reputación, experiencia, solvencia financiera y servicio al cliente. Evaluar adecuadamente a las aseguradoras y brokers es un paso esencial para garantizar que tu empresa reciba la cobertura más adecuada y confiable para sus necesidades logísticas. 1. Reputación y solvencia financiera La reputación y la solvencia financiera de un proveedor de seguros son factores determinantes en la elección de una aseguradora de carga. La reputación es una medida de la confianza y fiabilidad que otros clientes han depositado en la empresa, mientras que la solvencia financiera refleja la capacidad de la aseguradora para cumplir con sus obligaciones, especialmente en situaciones de crisis o grandes siniestros. Es fundamental investigar la estabilidad financiera del proveedor para asegurarte de que no solo podrá pagar las reclamaciones, sino también responder en situaciones complicadas o en caso de siniestros significativos. Para esto, puedes consultar las calificaciones emitidas por agencias reconocidas como AM Best, Standard & Poor’s o Moody’s, que ofrecen evaluaciones independientes sobre la solidez financiera de las compañías aseguradoras. Estas clasificaciones te proporcionan una visión clara de si la aseguradora tiene los recursos necesarios para manejar grandes pérdidas o desastres. Además, puedes buscar reseñas y testimonios de clientes actuales o anteriores para tener una idea del historial del proveedor. Foros especializados en logística y transporte de carga también pueden ser valiosas fuentes de información sobre cómo los proveedores manejan los siniestros y su compromiso a largo plazo con los clientes. 2. Servicio al cliente y soporte El nivel de servicio al cliente y soporte que una aseguradora puede ofrecer es igualmente crucial. En el transporte de carga, donde los imprevistos pueden surgir en cualquier momento, contar con un proveedor que ofrezca una atención al cliente eficiente y disponible las 24 horas del día es esencial. La capacidad de resolver problemas, dudas o reclamaciones con rapidez y claridad es un factor que puede marcar la diferencia entre una operación exitosa y una que enfrenta grandes complicaciones. Debes verificar que el proveedor ofrezca soporte 24/7, especialmente si tu empresa opera a nivel internacional, donde las diferencias de zonas horarias pueden hacer que la atención inmediata sea indispensable. Además, es útil contar con un equipo de soporte especializado en seguros de carga, con experiencia en los detalles del transporte de mercancías por mar, aire y tierra. El conocimiento profundo del sector logístico permite que el equipo de atención al cliente pueda asesorarte sobre la mejor cobertura para tu tipo de mercancía y ofrecer soluciones proactivas ante posibles problemas. 3. Velocidad en el proceso de reclamación Un proceso de reclamación ágil es uno de los principales aspectos que debes evaluar al elegir un proveedor de seguros de carga. El transporte de mercancías opera bajo calendarios ajustados, y un retraso en la resolución de una reclamación puede generar costos adicionales, como interrupciones en la cadena de suministro, penalidades contractuales o pérdida de clientes. Por lo tanto, es crucial que la aseguradora tenga políticas claras y eficientes para manejar reclamaciones de manera rápida y sin complicaciones. Al seleccionar un proveedor, es recomendable revisar cuánto tiempo tarda en promedio en procesar y pagar una reclamación, y si tienen una política de plazos específicos para ciertos tipos de siniestros. Una aseguradora con un proceso lento de reclamaciones puede crear problemas operativos a tu empresa, por lo que es preferible optar por aquellas que ofrezcan tiempos de resolución cortos y una comunicación clara durante todo el proceso. Es aconsejable también indagar sobre el nivel de digitalización del proveedor. Aseguradoras que permiten presentar reclamaciones y seguir el progreso del caso a través de plataformas digitales o aplicaciones móviles ofrecen una ventaja significativa, ya que agilizan el proceso y reducen la burocracia. Esto también mejora la experiencia del cliente, ya que permite una mejor gestión del tiempo y evita complicaciones adicionales durante la tramitación. Tipos de seguros de carga: ¿qué opciones existen? Al cotizar seguros de carga, encontrarás diferentes tipos de pólizas que varían en cobertura y costos. Conocer las opciones disponibles te permitirá elegir la más adecuada para tu negocio. 1. Seguro de todo riesgo Esta póliza es la más completa, ya que cubre prácticamente todos los riesgos asociados con el transporte de mercancías, a menos que se especifiquen exclusiones. Cubre daños o pérdidas por causas externas, como robos, accidentes, catástrofes naturales o mal manejo de la carga. 2. Seguro contra riesgos nombrados A diferencia del seguro de todo riesgo, esta póliza solo cubre los riesgos explícitamente mencionados en la póliza. Aunque tiene primas más bajas, la cobertura es más limitada. Este tipo de seguro es adecuado para empresas que transportan mercancías con menos riesgo o que buscan una opción más económica. 3. Seguro de responsabilidad civil Este seguro cubre la responsabilidad del transportista en caso de pérdida o daño de la mercancía, pero no ofrece cobertura directa sobre los bienes. Es importante notar que la cobertura de responsabilidad civil puede no ser suficiente para proteger completamente los intereses del propietario de la carga. ¿Cómo solicitar y comparar cotizaciones? El proceso de cotización de un seguro de carga puede variar de un proveedor a otro. Sin embargo, hay algunos pasos comunes que debes seguir para obtener cotizaciones adecuadas y compararlas de manera efectiva: 1. Recolección de información Para que las aseguradoras puedan proporcionarte una cotización precisa, deberás proporcionar información detallada sobre tu operación logística. Algunos de los datos que te solicitarán incluyen: Tipo de mercancía. Valor de la mercancía. Medio de transporte (aéreo, terrestre o marítimo). Distancia y rutas del transporte. Historial de reclamaciones anteriores (si aplica). 2. Comparación de cotizaciones Una vez que hayas solicitado varias cotizaciones, es importante hacer una comparación exhaustiva no solo del costo, sino también de las coberturas, exclusiones y servicios adicionales que cada póliza ofrece. Es recomendable no elegir solo en función del precio más bajo, sino considerando la relación calidad-precio y qué tan bien cubre la póliza las necesidades específicas de tu negocio. 3. Negociación de términos En algunos casos, es posible negociar ciertos términos de la póliza, como los deducibles, los plazos de pago o las exclusiones. Si tienes un buen historial como cliente y manejas volúmenes importantes de transporte, puedes obtener mejores condiciones. Retorno de Inversión (ROI) en el seguro de carga Contratar un seguro de carga no es solo un gasto, sino una inversión. Proteger tu mercancía y tus operaciones logísticas contra posibles pérdidas o daños puede generar un retorno significativo a largo plazo. Las empresas que operan sin seguro o con un seguro inadecuado corren el riesgo de sufrir pérdidas financieras graves en caso de un siniestro. Casos de éxito en la elección de seguros de carga Un ejemplo de la importancia de seleccionar correctamente un seguro de carga es el caso de una empresa exportadora de productos electrónicos que sufrió el robo de uno de sus contenedores durante el transporte marítimo. Gracias a una póliza de seguro de todo riesgo, la empresa pudo recuperar el valor total de su mercancía en un plazo de 30 días, evitando así pérdidas económicas significativas y manteniendo su relación con sus clientes. Conclusión: cómo elegir la mejor cotización de un seguro de carga Elegir la mejor cotización de un seguro de carga es un proceso que requiere un análisis detallado de las coberturas, exclusiones, costos y características del proveedor de seguros. La clave es no solo enfocarse en el precio, sino en la calidad y amplitud de la cobertura que protegerá tu mercancía y tus operaciones. Un seguro adecuado te permitirá operar con tranquilidad y garantizar la continuidad de tu negocio, incluso en situaciones adversas. En Nowports, entendemos la importancia de encontrar la solución adecuada para proteger tus envíos y minimizar riesgos en cada paso de la cadena de suministro. Nuestro equipo de expertos te guiará para elegir la cobertura más completa y personalizada, asegurando que cada detalle de tu operación esté respaldado por una protección sólida y confiable.

title: CLAUDE.md Best Practices: The 10-Section Template That Makes Claude Code 10x Better
summary: CLAUDE.md is the most underused feature in Claude Code. Here's the exact template and 10 sections that power users use to eliminate repeated mistakes and get consistent results.
body_text: Section 1: Project Overview (2-4 sentences) What is this project? Who uses it? What's the main thing it does? ## Project Overview MyApp is a B2B SaaS tool for restaurant managers. It tracks inventory, generates purchase orders, and forecasts needs based on historical usage. About 200 paying restaurants use it daily. The codebase has been live since 2024. This tells Claude Code: this is a production system with real users, not a toy project. It will be more conservative about changes. Section 2: Tech Stack (list format) ## Tech Stack - Runtime: Node.js 20, TypeScript (strict mode) - Framework: Express 4 - Database: PostgreSQL 15 via Prisma ORM - Auth: Clerk - Testing: Jest + Supertest - Package manager: npm (not yarn, not pnpm) - Deployment: Railway - Key libraries: zod (validation), dayjs (dates), winston (logging) Explicit stack listing prevents the agent from suggesting React when you use Vue, or recommending a library you've already rejected. Section 3: Architecture Rules This is the highest-impact section. Document the decisions you've already made so the agent respects them. ## Architecture Rules - ALL database queries go in /services — never in /routes, /middleware, or /utils - ALL input validation goes in /middleware/validate.ts before routes run - /routes should contain ONLY: auth check, input forwarding, service call, response formatting - /utils contains ONLY stateless helper functions (no DB, no external APIs) - Error handling: throw from services, catch in routes, never swallow errors silently - Never use direct SQL strings — always use Prisma ORM methods - Database transactions: use prisma.$transaction() for multi-step writes Without this, Claude Code will "helpfully" put a database query in a route because it's faster to write. With this, it knows that's a violation. Section 4: Coding Standards ## Coding Standards - All public functions: JSDoc comments with @param, @returns, @throws - Error messages: user-facing only (no stack traces, no internal IDs in API responses) - Async: always async/await, never .then() chaining - Imports: absolute imports from src/ root, not relative (import { User } from 'models/user') - No console.log: use winston logger (logger.info, logger.warn, logger.error) - ESLint + Prettier auto-run on file save (configured in .eslintrc and .prettierrc — don't change these) - All new API endpoints must have rate limiting middleware Section 5: Testing Requirements ## Testing Requirements - New service functions: unit tests required before PR - New API endpoints: integration tests required before PR - Test file location: /tests/unit/ for units, /tests/integration/ for routes - Test file naming: [ filename ].test.ts matching source file name - Run tests: `npm test` - Coverage minimum: 80% on new code (CI enforced) - Do NOT run `npm run test:integration` without a local DB running This prevents the agent from writing tests in the wrong place, with the wrong naming, or from running a test command that would fail without a database. Section 6: Build and Run Commands ## Build and Run Commands - Dev server: `npm run dev` (port 3000, hot reload) - Build: `npm run build` — ⚠️ DO NOT run this; it takes 4 minutes and breaks the dev server. Only CI runs builds. - Test: `npm test` - Database migrations: `npm run db:migrate` (runs Prisma migrations) - Seed database: `npm run db:seed` (local only, never production) - Lint: `npm run lint` - Type check: `npm run typecheck` The warning on npm run build is there because agents will run build commands without being asked if they're not told not to. This prevents a common annoying workflow interruption. The 'What NOT to Do' section is the most protective part of CLAUDE.md — document your anti-patterns explicitly Blink Section 7: External Services ## External Services - Stripe: used for subscription billing. Webhooks in /routes/stripe-webhook.ts. Never modify this without testing in Stripe CLI first. - SendGrid: for transactional emails. Templates in /emails/. Don't hard-code email addresses. - Cloudflare R2: object storage for receipts. Helper at /lib/storage.ts. Use this helper, never call the S3 SDK directly. - Redis: session caching and rate limiting. Connection in /lib/redis.ts. Environment variables: see .env.example. Local dev uses .env.local. Production uses Railway env vars. Section 8: What NOT to Do Document the anti-patterns you've already fought and fixed. This is the most underutilized section. ## What NOT to Do - Do NOT use setTimeout for retry logic — use the `retryWithBackoff` helper in /utils/retry.ts - Do NOT add console.log for debugging — use the logger and remove debug logs before committing - Do NOT use Prisma's `raw` queries — use the ORM. The one exception is /scripts/analytics.ts (documented there) - Do NOT modify /middleware/errorHandler.ts without reading error-handling.md in /docs first - Do NOT create new Stripe Price IDs in code — update via Stripe dashboard, reference by env var - Do NOT store user PII in logs (emails, phone numbers, payment data) - Do NOT run `git push --force` on main Every item in this list was learned the hard way by your team. Document it so the agent (and new team members) don't make the same mistake. Section 9: Context Shortcuts Define project-specific terms the agent should know: ## Context Shortcuts - "the client" = Acme Corp (our biggest enterprise customer) - "the new flow" = the redesigned onboarding flow (in /features/onboarding-v2) - "legacy auth" = the old JWT-based auth in /auth-legacy (being phased out, do not add to it) - "the metrics endpoint" = GET /api/internal/metrics (internal only, not exposed externally) - "the dashboard" = /pages/dashboard.tsx (user-facing, high traffic, performance-sensitive) This prevents "I need to fix the dashboard" from being ambiguous. Section 10: Ongoing Work ## Ongoing Work (as of April 2026) - Active refactor: moving from JWT auth to Clerk (see MIGRATION.md for details) - Old auth in /auth-legacy — do not add new endpoints to this - New auth in /middleware/clerk.ts — use this for all new endpoints - Known issue: the inventory forecast job sometimes times out on large datasets (>10k items). This is tracked in issue #1247. body_text: If your organization runs on NetSuite, a NetSuite connector is what closes the gap between your ERP and the tools your team uses to report, analyze, and act on that data. Think of it as a bridge. Your financial data, your order records, your customer and vendor transactions: all of it lives inside NetSuite. The connector is what lets your analytics platform, your reporting workflow, or your automation pipeline pull that data on demand, without anyone having to export a file, paste numbers into a spreadsheet, or wait on IT to run a query. For finance and operations teams that spend the first half of every week gathering data before they can do anything with it, a well-configured NetSuite connection can be the difference between reporting that runs itself and reporting that consumes the people who are supposed to be doing something more valuable. What a NetSuite Connector Actually Does When you set up a NetSuite connector, you are giving your analytics or automation platform permission to access your ERP and extract the records your workflows depend on. You authenticate with your NetSuite account, specify which modules, saved searches, or records are relevant (financials, inventory, sales orders, customers, vendors, or all of the above) and the connection handles the rest. From that point on, your platform can query NetSuite on a schedule you define without anyone having to log in, navigate menus, or trigger a manual export. The data flows directly into your reports, models, and pipelines as if it had always been there. The best NetSuite connectors are built so that finance and operations analysts, not just developers or NetSuite administrators, can configure and manage them. You should be able to point to the records you need, define the refresh cadence, and start building a workflow without writing SuiteScript or submitting a support ticket. Once the connection is live, it should stay live: refreshing on schedule, picking up new transactions automatically, and alerting you if something falls out of sync. For a finance team that needs consolidated reporting ready by Tuesday morning, that reliability is not a nice-to-have. It is the whole point. What Finance and Operations Teams Actually Need From a NetSuite Integration The analysts who feel the absence of proper NetSuite integration most sharply are the ones sitting between the ERP and the business: finance managers building consolidation reports, FP&A analysts tracking actuals against budgets, operations leads monitoring fulfillment metrics. They know their way around NetSuite well enough to pull what they need, and they understand the data well enough to build and maintain the reports their organization depends on. What they are missing is not access. It is the layer that takes what they have access to and turns it into something reliable, automated, and consistent. The problem shows up in the same pattern across industries. A finance team might pull revenue and expense data from NetSuite, cross-reference it with headcount data from an HR system, apply allocation logic that lives in a shared spreadsheet, and deliver a formatted management report every month-end close. A supply chain team might extract open purchase orders and inventory positions from NetSuite, layer in supplier lead times from a separate file, and produce a replenishment forecast in Excel for the operations review. Each step in those workflows is manual, each step introduces the possibility of error, and the entire process has to be reconstructed from memory whenever someone is out or leaves the team. The NetSuite connector is the entry point. The automation layer on top of it is what makes those workflows reliable and repeatable. What This Looks Like in Practice Consider a corporate finance team at a mid-sized consumer goods company. They close the books in NetSuite and maintain a set of recurring reports that pull actuals from the ERP, compare them against budgets maintained in Excel, and layer in commentary from business unit leads before formatting everything into a PowerPoint deck for the board. The ERP is the system of record. But the reporting workflow that sits on top of it is a patchwork of manual exports, vlookups, and slide-by-slide formatting that consumes three days of analyst time every month time that is nominally about reporting but is actually about data assembly. When a team like this adds a proper automation layer on top of their NetSuite connector, the workflow changes fundamentally. The data pull from NetSuite runs automatically at close. The reconciliation logic (the joins to the budget file, the variance calculations, the segment roll-ups) is encoded once and applied consistently every period. The reporting agent formats the output directly into the board template, populating tables, charts, and commentary placeholders without anyone touching a slide. The analyst who used to spend three days assembling data now spends a few hours reviewing output, adding judgment, and preparing for the conversation. That shift from data assembly to data interpretation is where the value of a well-integrated NetSuite connection actually lives. What to Look for in a NetSuite Connector When evaluating a NetSuite connector or the platform it is part of, the first question to ask is whether it works with NetSuite alone or alongside every other source your workflows depend on. Most finance and operations reports pull from more than one place. You might have financials in NetSuite, headcount in Workday, pipeline in Salesforce, and budget models in Excel, all of which need to come together in a single deliverable. A connector that handles NetSuite but leaves the rest to manual exports has not solved the problem. It has just made one step slightly easier. Look for a platform where NetSuite is one of many integrated sources, not the only one. The second question is what the platform does with the data after it pulls it. Getting data out of NetSuite is the starting point, not the finish line. You want a platform that can combine your NetSuite records with other sources, apply the business logic and allocation rules your reports depend on, and keep that logic consistent every time the report runs, without someone having to redo it manually each period. The goal is a workflow where the hard work of preparing data happens once, is saved, and runs automatically going forward. Third, think about where the data ends up. Dashboards are useful, but most finance and operations teams also need reports in Excel, presentations in PowerPoint, or documents formatted for a specific audience. If the platform can take your NetSuite data, apply your business logic, and write the results directly into a formatted Excel file or board deck, that is a very different outcome from a tool that gets you as far as a dashboard and leaves the last mile to you. Finally, consider how much technical support the platform requires to operate. A NetSuite integration that needs a developer every time you want to change the report structure, add a new field, or onboard a new data source will always be a bottleneck. The best platforms let analysts configure and modify their own workflows, ask questions of the data in plain language, and get answers without filing a ticket or waiting on someone with NetSuite admin access. How Redbird Connects to NetSuite and the Rest of Your Data Ecosystem Redbird is an agentic AI data platform that connects to NetSuite as part of a broader connectivity layer spanning ERP systems including SAP and Oracle, cloud data warehouses, SaaS platforms including Salesforce, Workday, Google Analytics, and advertising platforms, file-based sources, and legacy systems where no standard API exists. The NetSuite connector is one piece of a platform designed to automate the full data lifecycle: from ingestion and transformation through advanced analytics and production-ready output delivery. When a user connects NetSuite to Redbird, they are not just enabling data access. They are bringing the ERP into an environment where specialized AI agents handle every step of the workflow that follows. A Data Collection Agent pulls from NetSuite and every other configured source. A Data Engineering Agent harmonizes the data, applies transformations, and ensures the output is clean and analysis-ready. An Analyst Agent computes custom metrics and applies business logic including period-over-period comparisons, budget variances, cost allocations, and segment roll-ups. A Reporting Agent assembles the final deliverable in the format the team actually uses, whether that is an Excel file, a PowerPoint presentation, or a live dashboard, using existing templates and standards. All of this runs on a scheduled cadence without manual intervention, and every step of every workflow is fully auditable. What makes this architecture meaningful in practice is that it compresses timelines that typically take days into minutes. Teams that used to spend 60 to 80 percent of their analyst time on data preparation report dramatically less time doing that work after deploying Redbird. That time does not disappear. It moves upstream, into interpretation, variance analysis, and the kind of financial thinking that actually requires human judgment. Redbird works with organizations across financial services, media, consumer goods, and technology, including eight of the Fortune 50, in environments where the accuracy, auditability, and control requirements are among the most demanding in the world. The Bottom Line The right NetSuite connector is not just a data tap. It is the foundation of how your team gets from raw ERP data to finished, accurate reports. It should connect to the other sources your workflows depend on, keep your data current on a schedule, and sit inside a platform that handles the logic, the validation, and the delivery without manual work in between. The teams that get the most out of their ERP investment are the ones who have built, or found, an automation layer that handles everything that happens after the data pull: the joins, the transformations, the calculations, and the delivery of outputs that people can actually use. If your analysts are still spending the majority of their time preparing data rather than analyzing it, the question is not whether your NetSuite connection is working. It is whether the workflow built on top of it is working as hard as it should be.

title: Trends in Semiconductor Manufacturing: Wafer-Level and Panel-Level Packaging
summary: Learn more about the trends in semiconductor manufacturing, with an emphasis on wafer-level packaging, from the experts at ACM Research
body_text: One of the most important shifts in semiconductor manufacturing today is not just the continued growth of wafer-level packaging (WLP), but the increasing reliance on enabling, highly specialized process technologies. As device architectures evolve toward heterogeneous integration (HI) and chiplet-based designs, key technologies such as wet processing, electrochemical plating (ECP), plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD), and emerging panel-level packaging (PLP) have become central to achieving the required levels of precision, performance, and scalability. WLP remains a cornerstone of advanced packaging (AP), encompassing integration approaches such as fan-in and fan-out, as well as 2D, 2.5D, and 3D architectures. But increasingly, it is the process technologies behind these approaches that are defining success. High-aspect-ratio through-silicon vias (TSVs), ultra-fine redistribution layers (RDLs), and advanced interconnect schemes depend on tightly controlled deposition, plating, cleaning, and surface preparation steps. While PLP is gaining traction as a complementary path to scale, it introduces new challenges in uniformity, materials handling, and process integration. This further underscores the importance of technologies that can deliver consistent results across larger substrates: plating enables uniform metal fill, PECVD supports conformal dielectric deposition and passivation, and advanced wet processing ensures contamination control and surface readiness across complex topographies. These process-driven innovations are what ultimately make it possible to extend Moore’s Law through heterogeneous integration, enabling improvements in power, performance, area, and cost. Technology Trend Drivers Demand for AI, 5G, high-performance computing (HPC), and advanced consumer electronics continues to accelerate – in turn, driving the need for packaging technologies that can integrate more functionality into smaller footprints. This demand is not only increasing the adoption of WLP and PLP, but also pushing process technologies to new limits. Achieving tighter line/space geometries, higher interconnect densities, and improved reliability requires a level of precision and repeatability that only advanced wet processing, plating, and deposition systems can provide. At the same time, sustainability has become a parallel driver. Semiconductor manufacturers are under increasing pressure to reduce chemical consumption, minimize waste, and improve overall process efficiency. This is especially relevant for wet and plating processes, which traditionally consume significant volumes of chemicals and water. As a result, there is a growing emphasis on closed-loop systems, chemical recycling, and process optimization—ensuring that high-volume manufacturing (HVM) can be both economically and environmentally sustainable. Front-End Advanced Packaging Process Control Unlike traditional chip-packaging approaches, in WLP—and increasingly in PLP—everything from chip fabrication to assembly, inspection, and test is moving toward front-end-like process rigor. As devices continue to shrink and interconnect density increases, many of the processes being used are no longer simplified adaptations, but rather direct extensions of front-end wafer processing technologies. Over the past few decades, one of the trends in semiconductor manufacturing was the proliferation of new tool suppliers who carved a niche by developing packaging-specific tools targeted primarily at OSATs. These tools supported processes such as electrochemical plating for Cu bumping and RDL formation, wet processing for coating, developing, stripping, and etching, and, to a lesser extent, dielectric deposition. This approach worked well for earlier generations of WLP built on legacy nodes, where process tolerances were more forgiving. However, as advanced packaging has evolved to include finer RDL line/space, high-aspect-ratio TSVs, hybrid bonding, and larger panel formats, those earlier tools are increasingly unable to meet the requirements for uniformity, defect control, and repeatability. Today, advanced packagingflows require front-end-level precision across multiple process steps. For example: Electrochemical plating must deliver void-free fill in deep TSVs and uniform pillar heights across the wafer or panel. Wet processing must ensure ultra-clean, particle-free surfaces for subsequent deposition and bonding steps. PECVD is playing an expanding role in depositing high-quality dielectric films for passivation, insulation, and stress control in both wafer- and panel-level flows. PLP integration demands consistent process performance across significantly larger substrates, amplifying any non-uniformities present at the wafer scale. The bottom line: advanced packagingprocesses are far less forgiving than before and require tightly integrated, high-performance toolsets that can bridge front-end capability with back-end cost sensitivity. H2: Panel-Level Packaging Process Innovation As PLP continues to gain momentum, it is further reshaping process requirements across the packaging ecosystem. While the promise of higher throughput and lower cost per unit is compelling, scaling processes from wafers to panels introduces new complexities in fluid dynamics, deposition uniformity, and materials compatibility. Wet processing and plating systems must be re-engineered to handle larger formats while maintaining tight control over chemistry distribution and process uniformity. Similarly, PECVD processes must ensure conformal film deposition across larger areas without compromising film quality or throughput. These challenges reinforce a broader industry shift: process innovation—not just packaging architecture—is becoming the primary advanced packagingdifferentiator. Our Advanced Packaging Solutions Support Sustainable HVM ACM Research has leveraged deep expertise in front-end semiconductor processing and extended it to address the evolving requirements of advanced packaging, including both wafer-level and panel-level applications. Our approach focuses on delivering front-end-grade performance while maintaining the cost efficiency required for high-volume manufacturing. For example, our electrochemical plating solutions are designed to address the challenges of filling high-aspect-ratio features with excellent uniformity and throughput. By optimizing mass transport and electric field distribution at the wafer level, these systems enable superior within-wafer and within-die uniformity, even for demanding TSV and RDL applications. Our advanced wet processing platforms support a wide range of critical steps, including cleaning, coating, developing, stripping, and etching. These systems are designed with closed-loop chemical management to reduce consumption and enable real-time recycling and reuse—supporting both sustainability goals and cost reduction. In addition, our capabilities extend to stress-free surface preparation and planarization processes that are essential for hybrid bonding and other advanced integration schemes. Achieving ultra-smooth, particle-free surfaces is critical for these applications, and integrating wet and dry process steps within a single platform enables greater process control and efficiency. What’s Next? Advanced packaging is no longer defined solely by architecture, but by the processes that enable it. As WLP and PLP continue to evolve, technologies such as wet processing, plating, and PECVD will play an even more critical role in determining device performance, manufacturing efficiency, and overall cost. By bringing our front-end expertise to back-end challenges, ACM helps the industry unlock the full potential of heterogeneous integration and continue to drive innovation across AI, 5G, HPC, and beyond. We continue to expand our portfolio to address emerging needs in PECVD and panel-level packaging, ensuring that customers can scale advanced packaging technologies without compromising performance, yield, or sustainability. To learn more about our full suite of process solutions for advanced packaging applications, connect with us at contact@acmr.com . Advanced Packaging Trends FAQs How has semiconductor packaging evolved over the past five years as the industry has moved beyond wafer-level packaging? While wafer-level packaging remains foundational, the past five years have seen a shift toward process-driven innovation to support heterogeneous integration and increasingly complex architectures. Technologies such as advanced wet processing, electrochemical plating, and plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) have become critical enablers of fine-pitch interconnects, through-silicon vias (TSVs), and redistribution layers. Rather being defined solely by structure (e.g., 2.5D or 3D), packaging success is now dictated by the precision, uniformity, and repeatability of these underlying processes. This evolution reflects a broader move toward front-end-like process control in advanced packaging. How have chiplet architectures changed semiconductor design in recent years? Chiplet architectures have accelerated the industry’s shift toward heterogeneous integration, requiring packaging technologies that can seamlessly integrate multiple dies into a single system. This has placed new demands on interconnect density, alignment accuracy, and surface preparation, making advanced process technologies essential to enabling reliable integration. As a result, design and manufacturing are now more tightly coupled, with packaging processes playing a central role in system performance. The rise of chiplets has reinforced the importance of precision-driven manufacturing approaches traditionally associated with front-end fabrication. How have the primary demand drivers for semiconductor packaging shifted over the past five years? Demand has increasingly been driven by applications such as AI, 5G, high-performance computing (HPC), and advanced consumer electronics, all of which require greater functionality in smaller footprints. This has pushed packaging technologies to deliver higher interconnect density, tighter geometries, and improved reliability. At the same time, sustainability has emerged as a parallel driver, with manufacturers focusing on reducing chemical usage, minimizing waste, and improving process efficiency. Together, these forces are reshaping both packaging architectures and the process technologies that support them. How has hybrid bonding advanced as a next-generation interconnect technology in semiconductor packaging? Hybrid bonding has advanced alongside improvements in surface preparation, planarization, and contamination control, all of which are critical to achieving reliable direct interconnects. The technology places stringent requirements on ultra-clean, particle-free, and highly planar surfaces, driving the need for tightly integrated wet and dry processing solutions. As interconnect pitches shrink and performance demands increase, hybrid bonding is becoming a key enabler of next-generation integration schemes. Its progress reflects the broader industry shift toward front-end-level precision in packaging processes. How have semiconductor packaging manufacturing formats evolved with the introduction of panel-level approaches? Panel-level packaging (PLP) has emerged as a complementary manufacturing format to wafers, offering the potential for higher throughput and lower cost per unit. However, scaling to larger rectangular substrates introduces new challenges in process uniformity, materials handling, and integration. Technologies such as plating, PECVD, and advanced wet processing must be re-engineered to maintain consistency across larger areas. As a result, PLP is not just a change in format, but a driver of innovation in process technology across the packaging ecosystem.
